extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political philosophy and moral theory (e.g., Hobbes' Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply Hobbesian criteria for what counts as honour, dignity, worthiness, the causes of manners, and the natural seeds and expressions of religion as set out in a political-philosophical treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring and Dishonouring (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honouring and Dishonouring are valuing another; to value a man at a high rate is to honour him, at a low rate is to dishonour him — high and low judged by comparison to the rate each man sets on himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret honour/dishonour relationally: it's the perceived valuation relative to the person's own self-assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity (public worth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignity is the public worth assigned to a person by the commonwealth, signified by offices of command, judicature, public employment, or by names and titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat official positions, titles, and public employments as primary markers of a person's dignity in civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praying as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: To pray to another for aid is to honour them because it shows belief in their power to help; more difficult aid requested implies greater honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use requests for help as a signal of perceived power; weight the difficulty of the request when judging degree of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: To obey is to honour, since no one obeys someone they think has no power to help or hurt them; conversely, disobedience is dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess obedience as recognition of power and therefore as an honouring act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts as Signals of Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving great gifts honours a man (buying protection/acknowledging power); giving little gifts is akin to alms and signifies dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between substantial gifts (honour/protection) and small gifts (charity/insult).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion/Flattery vs Neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: Being sedulous in promoting another's good, including flattering, is to honour (seeking protection); neglect is to dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize promotion and flattery as instrumental acts acknowledging someone’s power; contrast with omission of support as dishonour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding Place as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: To give way or place to another in any commodity is to honour them (confession of greater power); arrogating for oneself is dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relinquishing status/position to another as an admission of their superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing Love or Fear as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing signs of love or fear for someone is to honour them; to contemn or show less love/fear than expected is to dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional displays (love/fear) are evaluative signals of perceived value and power; failing expected displays is insulting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise vs Revile
rubrics_metrics.description: To praise, magnify, or call someone happy is to honour them; to revile, mock, or pity is to dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public verbal evaluation (praise vs mockery) functions as honour signalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful Conduct as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking to someone with consideration and appearing before them with decency and humility is honourable; rash speech or obscene/slovenly/impudent behaviour is dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess manners and decorum as indicators of honouring attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and Reliance as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: To believe, trust, or rely on another is to honour them; to distrust or not believe is to dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat trust as acknowledgment of virtue/power; distrust is a negative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attentive Listening as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: To hearken to a man's counsel or discourse is to honour him (sign of opinion of his wisdom/eloquence/wit); sleeping, leaving, or talking while he speaks is dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure honour by the quality of attention given to someone's speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing Customary Signs of Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing those things which another takes as signs of honour, or which law/custom makes so, is to honour; refusing to do them is dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect local/customary markers of honour even if they are conventional; refusal is an affront.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement as Honour; Dissent as Dishonour
rubrics_metrics.description: To agree with someone in opinion is to honour them (approving their judgment/wisdom); to dissent is to dishonour and to upbraid for error, especially if dissent is on many matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political/social conformity can be a form of honour; widespread dissent implies contempt/foolishness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating someone is to honour them (vehement approval); but to imitate one's enemy is dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation is a strong signal of approval—context (who is imitated) matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring Another's Honours
rubrics_metrics.description: To honour those another honours is to honour that person (sign of approbation of his judgment); to honour his enemies is to dishonour him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal honouring networks reinforce perceived wisdom/power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment in Counsel as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: To employ someone in counsel or in actions of difficulty is to honour them (sign of opinion of their wisdom or other power); to deny such employment to seekers is dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments to responsibilities are concrete manifestations of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's Power to Confer Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereign honours a subject by whatever title, office, employment, or action he chooses to use as a sign of honour (sovereign can institute signs of honour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Persian king honoring Mordecai with public procession; sovereigns can manipulate honour through ceremonial grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour as Sign of Power
rubrics_metrics.description: What is honourable is whatever possession, action, or quality serves as an argument and sign of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate honour by whether something indicates or augments an individual's power in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being Honoured/Loved/Feared of Many
rubrics_metrics.description: To be honoured, loved, or feared by many is honourable because they are arguments of power; being honoured by few or none is dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social scale of recognition (many vs few) matters for honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune and Wealth as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Good fortune (if lasting) and riches are honourable as signs of divine favour or of power; ill fortune and poverty are dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material success is read as public sign of merit/power regardless of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues and Vices as Honour/Dishonour
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnanimity, liberality, hope, courage, confidence are honourable (proceed from conscience of power); pusillanimity, parsimony, fear, diffidence are dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral traits that manifest confidence and largeness of spirit are esteemed as honourable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely Resolution vs Irresolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely resolution/decision is honourable (contempt of small difficulties); irresolution is dishonourable and shows pusillanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to resolve within available time signals overattachment to trifles; decisive action is honoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of Speech/Action Determines Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions and speeches that proceed or seem to proceed from much experience, science, discretion, or wit are honourable; those from error, ignorance, or folly are dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess provenance of actions (wisdom vs ignorance) to determine honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic Gravity vs Feigned Gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravity (seriousness) that seems to come from a mind employed on something is honourable; gravity intended merely to appear grave is dishonourable (compared to a ship ballasted with sand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine seriousness (substance) from mere posturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuousness vs Obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Being conspicuous (known for wealth, office, great actions) is honourable as a sign of power; obscurity is dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public eminence functions as a sign of power and thus honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble Descent as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Being descended from conspicuous parents is honourable because of inherited aids and friends; obscure parentage is dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lineage and inherited social capital act as markers of honour in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity with Loss as Honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions proceeding from equity joined with loss are honourable (signs of magnanimity); craft, shifting, and neglect of equity are dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether moral actions cost the actor; costly equity signals true honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour Independent of Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an action is just or unjust does not alter its honourability; honour consists solely in the opinion of power, not in justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate moral rightness with honour; celebrated strength (even in unjust acts) can be honoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary Coats and Gentry
rubrics_metrics.description: Scutchions and hereditary coats of arms are honourable only when they carry eminent privileges, riches, or other power; otherwise not truly honourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic trappings count as honour only to the extent they denote real power or privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of Honour (origins and meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles such as Duke, Count, Marquis, Baron are honourable as they signify the value set by sovereign power; many titles originated as offices of command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat titles as institutional markers of honour whose original functions may explain their current prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthinesse/Fitnesse (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Worthinesse differs from worth or merit and consists in a particular power or ability for that of which a person is said to be worthy — usually named fitness or aptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess candidates for roles by specific aptitudes for those roles rather than by general merit or desert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit for Office vs Meritorious Right
rubrics_metrics.description: One may be worthiest to be commander or judge by fitness but still lack a right to the position; merit presupposes a right (promise), while worthiness is aptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate normative claims of right/entitlement from pragmatic claims of fitness for effective function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual Desire of Power
rubrics_metrics.description: A general human inclination is a perpetual and restless desire of power after power that ceases only in death, driven by need to assure means to live well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use desire for increasing power as explanatory principle for many social behaviours and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition Breeds Contention
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition for riches, honour, command, or other power inclines men to contention, enmity, and war because one competitor’s gain is another's loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rivalries and conflict where limited prizes of social value are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Obedience from Love of Ease
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of ease and sensual delight disposes men to obey a common power because they prefer protection over reliance on their own labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess obedience as rational concession in service of comfort and reduced effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience from Fear of Death or Wounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of death and wounds also disposes men to obey a common power; conversely, needy, hardy, or military-ambitious men are inclined to stir up war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear is a primary motive for seeking civil peace; certain dispositions counteract this motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience from Love of Arts and Leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of knowledge and arts inclines men to obey a common power because those desires contain a love of leisure and thus a need for protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/educational pursuits create incentives for stable governance that secures leisure time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of Virtue from Love of Praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire of praise disposes men to laudable actions to please those whose judgment they value; desire for fame after death likewise motivates present conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social esteem and reputation operate as motivators for ostensibly virtuous behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred from Inability to Requite Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving greater benefits from an equal than one can hope to requite disposes the receiver to counterfeit love but secretly to hatred; benefits from a superior incline to gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider power relations when interpreting the social effects of gift-giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred from Conscience of Deserving Hate
rubrics_metrics.description: Having done more hurt than can be expiated inclines the doer to hate the sufferer, anticipating revenge or forgiveness, both hateful prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral culpability and fear of retribution shape interpersonal animosities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness to Hurt from Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of oppression disposes a man to anticipate harm or to seek aid via society; preemptive violence is a rational response to perceived threat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-protective aggression stems from anticipatory fear in insecure contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust of Own Wit Favors Immediate Strike
rubrics_metrics.description: Men who distrust their own subtlety are more disposed in tumult and sedition to strike first rather than rely on cunning; those confident in wit prefer consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological self-assessment (trust in cunning) predicts tendency toward rashness or deliberation in conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vain-Glory Effects on Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Vain-glorious men who falsely imagine themselves gallant incline to ostentation but not to attempt; those whose sufficiency rests on flattery may rashly engage but retreat under danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different forms of vanity produce different behavioural failures—posture vs collapse under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition from Opinion of Sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Men with a strong opinion of their own wisdom in matters of government are inclined to ambition because public employment preserves the honour of their wisdom; eloquence fosters this opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oratory and self-opinion combine to produce political ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irresolution from Overvaluing Trifles
rubrics_metrics.description: Pusillanimity leads to irresolution and loss of opportunities; when deliberation runs until action time without clarity, failure to decide shows overvaluation of small matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness and ability to prioritize major over minor considerations are marks of courage/honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality Weakens Collective Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Frugality (though a virtue for the poor) makes a man unfit for actions requiring many people because it weakens endeavour, which depends on being nourished and rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh private thrift against public capacity to sustain organized collective efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence in Others from Ignorance of Marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the marks of wisdom and kindness (eloquence, flattery, military reputation) disposes men to confide in those who display them; these marks provide caution against danger and attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize ostensible signs of virtue; rhetorical skill can mislead trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on Authority from Ignorance of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Want of scientific knowledge (ignorance of causes) constrains a man to rely on the advice and authority of others when truth concerns him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of causal understanding predicts deference to perceived experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of Words Causes Credulity and Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the signification of words (lack of understanding) disposes men to accept falsehoods and nonsense and to give different names to the same thing depending on passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision of language and conceptual clarity are prerequisites for rational judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Custom from Ignorance of Right and Wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the causes and origins of Right, Equity, Law, and Justice disposes men to make custom and example the rule of their actions, calling unjust what custom punished and just what custom approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/customary orthodoxy often substitutes for reason in societies lacking causal understanding of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Private Men from Ignorance of Causes of Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of remote causes causes people to attribute all events to immediate causes and to adhere to private men who criticize public officials, even to the point of attacking supreme authority out of fear of punishment or shame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misattribution of blame to proximate agents (tax gatherers) fosters populist attachment and misdirected resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credulity from Ignorance of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of natural causes disposes a man to credulity, making him believe impossibilities; credulity in turn inclines to lying and inventing falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of natural-scientific understanding breeds superstition and mendacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity from Anxiety about Future
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxiety for future time disposes men to enquire into the causes of things because knowledge of causes helps order the present for future advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curiosity is instrumentally motivated by prudential concerns about future states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Seeds of Religion (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four natural seeds of religion: (1) opinion of ghosts, (2) ignorance of second causes, (3) devotion toward what men fear, (4) taking casual occurrences for prognostications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four as diagnostic categories for the emergence and variation of religious beliefs and ceremonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion Peculiar to Man (causal grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is peculiar to man because of: (1) desire to know causes, (2) taking beginnings to imply causes, (3) memory/observation of sequences leading to inference of causes; these produce anxiety and thus religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain religious belief as rooted in human cognitive capacities (curiosity, memory) plus anxiety about future events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of Invisible Agents and Incorporeality
rubrics_metrics.description: Men imagine invisible agents as like the soul or apparitions (ghosts) and suppose them incorporeal; because they cannot form an adequate idea of such incorporeal substance, they often call the divine incomprehensible rather than define it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand anthropomorphic projections and epistemic limits when analyzing beliefs about spirits/gods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worship Mirrors Human Honour Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Worship of invisible powers naturally takes forms analogous to honours paid to humans: gifts, petitions, thanks, submission of body, considerate addresses, swearing by invoking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rituals and ceremonial acts toward deities to parallel social acts of honour between people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of Extraordinary Events to Invisible Agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Men attribute extraordinary or future events to invisible agents by analogy to past coincidences, taking casual events or reputations as prognostications, which multiplies gods and ceremonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogate claims of divine signs as often arising from pattern-seeking on limited observations.
